questions.title: Which of the following best describes the characteristic feature of neurodegenerative diseases of the CNS?
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the characteristic feature of neurodegenerative diseases of the CNS?

options.A: Inflammation of neurons based on their physical location in the brain
options.B: Cellular degeneration of subsets of neurons related by function rather than physical location
options.C: Random destruction of all neuronal cell types equally
options.D: Primary involvement of glial cells with secondary neuronal damage

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neurodegenerative disease does not select neurons by anatomical location or produce an inflammatory reaction as its defining feature.
explanations.B: Correct. Neurodegenerative diseases selectively destroy neuron populations linked by shared function or connectivity, which is why a single disease can affect widely separated regions belonging to one functional network while sparing neighbouring neurons of a different class. This functional, not anatomical, selectivity underlies disease-specific patterns such as Braak staging in Alzheimer disease and the basal-ganglia-restricted loss seen in Parkinson disease. It distinguishes neurodegeneration from processes like infarction or abscess, which spread by contiguous anatomy instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neurodegeneration is selective, not a random or equal destruction of every neuronal cell type.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glial involvement is typically secondary/reactive (gliosis); the primary process targets neurons, not glia.

questions.learning_objective: State that neurodegenerative disease selects neurons by shared function/connectivity rather than by anatomical proximity.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 1.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT used to classify neurodegenerative diseases of the CNS?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT used to classify neurodegenerative diseases of the CNS?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS used). Clinical presentation — dementia versus movement disorder, for example — is a standard classification axis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS used). The accumulating protein (tau, alpha-synuclein, beta-amyloid, huntingtin) defines the 'proteinopathy' classification scheme.
explanations.C: Correct. Response to pharmacological treatment is not a recognised taxonomic criterion for neurodegenerative disease. Most of these diseases have no treatment that alters their course, and even where a drug provides partial symptomatic benefit (such as levodopa in Parkinson disease), that responsiveness is a management fact rather than a diagnostic classification criterion. Diseases are instead grouped by clinical syndrome, causative protein and genetics.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS used). Known genetic abnormalities (e.g. APP/PSEN mutations, CAG-repeat expansions) are a recognised classification axis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify pharmacological response as NOT a classification axis for neurodegenerative disease, unlike clinical presentation, protein type and genetics.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 2.

questions.title: Diseases affecting cerebral cortical neurons result in which of the following?
questions.question: Diseases affecting cerebral cortical neurons result in which of the following?

options.B: Loss of memory, language, insight, and planning

explanations.A: Incorrect. Movement disorders result from basal ganglia, not cerebral cortical, neurodegeneration.
explanations.B: Correct. Cerebral cortical neurodegeneration — as in Alzheimer disease and the frontotemporal dementias — produces the cortical dementia syndrome: progressive loss of memory, language function, insight and executive planning. This reflects the association-cortex functions these neurons subserve, in contrast to the movement or coordination syndromes produced by subcortical (basal ganglia or cerebellar) disease. It is the clinical hallmark used to localise a neurodegenerative process to the cortex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ataxia localises to the cerebellum, not the cerebral cortex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Muscle weakness reflects motor system (corticospinal tract/motor neuron) involvement, not association cortex loss.

questions.learning_objective: Link cortical neuron degeneration to the cognitive/dementia syndrome (memory, language, insight, planning loss).
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 3.

questions.title: What is the common pathological feature associated with many neurodegenerative disorders?
questions.question: What is the common pathological feature associated with many neurodegenerative disorders?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neurodegenerative disorders are not, as a class, viral in origin — that mechanism instead characterises certain CNS infections.
explanations.B: Correct. Most CNS neurodegenerative diseases share a common mechanism: misfolded or abnormally processed proteins accumulate within or around neurons and become toxic. Examples include beta-amyloid and tau in Alzheimer disease, alpha-synuclein in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia, and huntingtin in Huntington disease. This shared 'proteinopathy' mechanism links diseases with very different clinical pictures.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Autoimmune myelin destruction characterises demyelinating disease (e.g. multiple sclerosis), a distinct disease category from neurodegeneration.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ischaemic injury is a vascular mechanism, not the shared mechanism of the neurodegenerative disease group.

questions.learning_objective: State that abnormal protein accumulation is the shared pathological mechanism across most neurodegenerative disorders.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 8.

questions.title: Which statement about the classification of neurodegenerative diseases is CORRECT?
questions.question: Which statement about the classification of neurodegenerative diseases is CORRECT?

options.A: They can only be classified by their genetic abnormalities
options.B: They can be classified in multiple ways including clinical presentation and protein accumulation
options.C: They are classified solely based on the patient's age at onset
options.D: Classification is based only on response to treatment

explanations.A: Incorrect. Genetics is one axis among several, not the only one — clinical presentation and protein type are also used.
explanations.B: Correct. Neurodegenerative disease classification is multi-axial: clinical presentation (movement disorder versus dementia), the accumulating protein (tauopathy, synucleinopathy, amyloidopathy) and genetics are complementary, simultaneously valid schemes rather than competing alternatives. A single disease is typically described by more than one of these axes at once.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Age at onset is a clinical clue, not the sole classification basis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Treatment response is not a recognised classification axis for neurodegenerative disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that neurodegenerative disease classification is multi-axial (clinical presentation and protein accumulation both valid, not either/or).
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 9.

questions.title: Which disease category results in movement disorders?
questions.question: Which disease category results in movement disorders?

options.B: Diseases affecting neurons of the basal ganglia

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cortical neuron disease produces the cognitive/dementia syndrome, not primary movement disorder.
explanations.B: Correct. Neurodegeneration confined to the basal ganglia circuitry — caudate/putamen, globus pallidus and substantia nigra — produces the movement disorder syndromes, both hyperkinetic (e.g. Huntington disease) and akinetic-rigid (e.g. Parkinson disease), because these nuclei regulate voluntary motor output. This is the anatomical basis for the movement-disorder category of neurodegenerative disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cerebellar disease produces ataxia, a distinct category from the basal-ganglia movement disorders.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Motor neuron disease (e.g. ALS) produces weakness/wasting, not the basal-ganglia movement-disorder phenotype.

questions.learning_objective: Link basal ganglia neuron degeneration to the movement-disorder category of neurodegenerative disease.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 11.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a feature of diseases affecting cerebral cortical neurons?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a feature of diseases affecting cerebral cortical neurons?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a feature). Memory loss is a core feature of cortical neurodegeneration.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a feature). Language impairment is a core feature of cortical neurodegeneration.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a feature). Loss of insight is a core feature of cortical neurodegeneration.
explanations.D: Correct. Cortical neurodegeneration presents with the cognitive triad — memory, language and insight loss — reflecting association-cortex dysfunction. Muscle weakness is not part of this picture, because voluntary motor strength depends on the corticospinal tract, basal ganglia and motor unit rather than on association cortex integrity. A patient with both cognitive decline and weakness should prompt a search for a coexisting motor-system process, not be assumed to have a pure cortical disease.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude muscle weakness from the clinical feature set of cortical neurodegeneration, distinguishing it from motor system disease.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 12.

questions.title: Which of the following diseases is classified as a hyperkinetic movement disorder affecting the basal ganglia?
questions.question: Which of the following diseases is classified as a hyperkinetic movement disorder affecting the basal ganglia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parkinson disease is akinetic-rigid (hypokinetic), the opposite category.
explanations.B: Correct. Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG-repeat expansion disorder causing striatal (caudate/putamen) degeneration, producing chorea — the prototypical hyperkinetic movement disorder — together with cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance. It sits opposite Parkinson disease on the movement-disorder spectrum: hyperkinetic (excess movement) rather than akinetic-rigid (reduced movement). This hyperkinetic/akinetic-rigid distinction is the key classification axis being tested.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Multiple system atrophy (parkinsonian type) is akinetic-rigid, not hyperkinetic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progressive supranuclear palsy is an akinetic-rigid atypical parkinsonism, not hyperkinetic.

questions.learning_objective: Classify Huntington disease as a hyperkinetic basal ganglia movement disorder, contrasted with akinetic-rigid disease.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 4.

questions.title: Which of the following is classified as an akinetic-rigid disease predominantly affecting the substantia nigra?
questions.question: Which of the following is classified as an akinetic-rigid disease predominantly affecting the substantia nigra?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Huntington disease is hyperkinetic and striatal, the opposite category.
explanations.B: Correct. Parkinson disease results from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, producing the akinetic-rigid syndrome: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor and postural instability. It is the prototype of the akinetic-rigid (hypokinetic) movement disorder category, opposite the hyperkinetic disorders such as Huntington disease. The primary lesion is nigral dopaminergic loss, which then produces striatal dopamine deficiency.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Spinocerebellar ataxia degenerates cerebellar neurons, producing ataxia, not an akinetic-rigid syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ALS degenerates motor neurons, producing weakness, not an akinetic-rigid basal ganglia syndrome.

questions.learning_objective: Classify Parkinson disease as an akinetic-rigid disorder of the substantia nigra.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 7.

questions.title: Striatonigral degeneration is an example of which type of disorder?
questions.question: Striatonigral degeneration is an example of which type of disorder?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Striatonigral degeneration is a movement disorder, not a cortical dementia syndrome.
explanations.B: Correct. Striatonigral degeneration, the parkinsonian-predominant subtype of multiple system atrophy (MSA-P), causes combined striatal and nigral neurodegeneration and presents with an akinetic-rigid parkinsonian syndrome. It is typically poorly responsive to levodopa, an important 'atypical parkinsonism' red flag that distinguishes it clinically from idiopathic Parkinson disease despite sharing the same akinetic-rigid category. This poor treatment response, together with early autonomic or cerebellar features, helps clinicians suspect MSA over idiopathic Parkinson disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Striatonigral degeneration is akinetic-rigid, not hyperkinetic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cerebellar ataxia is a separate category; striatonigral degeneration is basal-ganglia (striatonigral) disease.

questions.learning_objective: Classify striatonigral degeneration within the akinetic-rigid disease category, as an atypical parkinsonism.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 13.

questions.title: Spinocerebellar ataxias result from degeneration of neurons in which structure?
questions.question: Spinocerebellar ataxias result from degeneration of neurons in which structure?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cerebral cortex degeneration produces cognitive decline, not ataxia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Basal ganglia degeneration produces movement disorders (hyperkinetic or akinetic-rigid), not ataxia.
explanations.C: Correct. The spinocerebellar ataxias are a group of inherited, typically trinucleotide-repeat, disorders causing progressive degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and associated spinocerebellar tract neurons. This produces the ataxia syndrome: gait and limb incoordination, dysarthria and nystagmus, localising the pathology specifically to the cerebellum rather than the basal ganglia or cerebral cortex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Motor cortex degeneration would produce weakness/spasticity, not ataxia.

questions.learning_objective: Localise spinocerebellar ataxia pathology to cerebellar neuron degeneration.

questions.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) results from degeneration of which type of neurons?
questions.question: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) results from degeneration of which type of neurons?

explanations.A: Incorrect. ALS classically spares sensory neurons — this is a key distinguishing feature from peripheral neuropathies with similar weakness.
explanations.B: Correct. ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that destroys both upper motor neurons (corticospinal tract) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells/brainstem motor nuclei), producing a combination of spasticity and flaccid weakness, fasciculations and muscle wasting. Sensory, cognitive and oculomotor function are typically spared, which helps distinguish ALS from other causes of progressive weakness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Autonomic neurons are not the primary target in typical ALS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ALS is defined by motor neuron loss specifically, not a generic interneuron process.

questions.learning_objective: State that ALS is a motor neuron disease, degenerating both upper and lower motor neurons.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Movement and coordination disorders
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 6.

questions.title: What is the crucial initiating event in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: What is the crucial initiating event in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease?

options.B: Accumulation of beta-amyloid peptide (Aβ) in the brain over time

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alpha-synuclein accumulation is the hallmark of Parkinson disease/Lewy body disease, not Alzheimer disease.
explanations.B: Correct. The amyloid cascade hypothesis holds that progressive cerebral accumulation of beta-amyloid (Aβ), generated by amyloidogenic cleavage of amyloid precursor protein, is the initiating event in Alzheimer disease. Aβ accumulation triggers downstream tau hyperphosphorylation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation and ultimately neuronal death. This positions Aβ as the pathogenic trigger rather than a bystander finding, and is the rationale behind anti-amyloid disease-modifying therapies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alzheimer disease is not primarily autoimmune; it is a proteinopathy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alzheimer disease is not caused by viral infection.

questions.learning_objective: State that progressive beta-amyloid accumulation is the crucial/initiating pathogenic event in Alzheimer disease.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 14.

questions.title: Which enzyme is NOT directly involved in the production of pathogenic Aβ from APP?
questions.question: Which enzyme is NOT directly involved in the production of pathogenic Aβ from APP?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS involved). BACE initiates the amyloidogenic pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS involved). γ-secretase completes cleavage in both the amyloidogenic and non-amyloidogenic pathways, releasing the final peptide.
explanations.C: Correct. Alpha-secretase cleaves APP within the Aβ domain itself, precluding formation of the full, pathogenic Aβ peptide and instead yielding non-toxic soluble fragments — the non-amyloidogenic pathway. This is the opposite role from BACE (β-secretase), which together with γ-secretase forms intact, aggregation-prone Aβ via the amyloidogenic pathway. Alpha-secretase activity is therefore protective, not pathogenic.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS involved). 'Beta-amyloid converting enzyme' is a synonym/distractor for BACE, which is amyloidogenic.

questions.learning_objective: Identify alpha-secretase as the enzyme that precludes pathogenic Abeta formation, unlike beta- and gamma-secretase.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 15.

questions.title: Mutations in which chromosome are associated with familial Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: Mutations in which chromosome are associated with familial Alzheimer's disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect for this item (PSEN1 is on chromosome 14, also a real familial AD gene, but the credited answer here is chromosome 21/APP).
explanations.B: Correct. Familial Alzheimer disease is linked to mutations in APP (chromosome 21), presenilin-1 (chromosome 14) and presenilin-2 (chromosome 1). The APP gene on chromosome 21 most directly explains increased amyloid production, and also explains the near-universal Alzheimer pathology seen in Down syndrome (trisomy 21), which effectively triples APP gene dosage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chromosome 19 carries the ApoE gene (risk factor for sporadic, not familial, Alzheimer disease), not a familial-AD-causing mutation.
explanations.D: Incorrect for this item (PSEN2 is on chromosome 1, also a real familial AD gene, but the credited answer here is chromosome 21/APP).

questions.learning_objective: Associate familial Alzheimer disease with chromosome 21 (APP gene), and its link to Down syndrome's amyloid pathology.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 16.

questions.title: What is the effect of Aβ deposits on neurons in Alzheimer disease?
questions.question: What is the effect of Aβ deposits on neurons in Alzheimer disease?

options.B: They are toxic to neurons and affect neurotransmission leading to neuronal death
options.C: They provide neuroprotection against oxidative stress

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aβ deposits are toxic, not regenerative.
explanations.B: Correct. Soluble Aβ oligomers and insoluble Aβ plaques disrupt synaptic function, impair neurotransmitter release and receptor signalling, promote oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and ultimately drive neuronal death. This neurotoxic effect — not any protective or regenerative action — is why Aβ accumulation is considered pathogenic rather than incidental.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aβ promotes oxidative stress; it does not protect against it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aβ impairs, rather than enhances, synaptic plasticity and neurotransmission.

questions.learning_objective: State that Abeta deposition is directly neurotoxic and impairs neurotransmission, rather than neuroprotective.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 17.

questions.title: The presence of Aβ leads to hyper-phosphorylation of which protein?
questions.question: The presence of Aβ leads to hyper-phosphorylation of which protein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alpha-synuclein aggregation is the synucleinopathy mechanism (Parkinson/Lewy body disease), not the downstream target of Aβ in Alzheimer disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prion protein misfolding is the mechanism of prion disease, unrelated to the Aβ-tau cascade.
explanations.C: Correct. Downstream of Aβ accumulation, intracellular signalling changes drive abnormal hyperphosphorylation of the microtubule-associated protein tau. This tau hyperphosphorylation is the second major pathological event of the amyloid cascade, linking extracellular Aβ plaques to the intracellular neurofibrillary tangle pathology of Alzheimer disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Huntingtin aggregation is the mechanism of Huntington disease, a CAG-repeat polyglutamine disorder unrelated to Aβ.

questions.learning_objective: Link beta-amyloid accumulation to downstream tau hyperphosphorylation in the amyloid cascade.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 18.

questions.title: What happens to tau protein after hyper-phosphorylation in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: What happens to tau protein after hyper-phosphorylation in Alzheimer's disease?

options.B: It redistributes from axons into dendrites and cell bodies, forming tangles

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperphosphorylated tau resists normal clearance and accumulates rather than being efficiently degraded.
explanations.B: Correct. Normal tau is an axonal, microtubule-stabilising protein. Once hyperphosphorylated, tau detaches from microtubules, mislocalises from the axon into the somatodendritic compartment, and self-aggregates into paired helical filaments that accumulate as neurofibrillary tangles. This mislocalisation-then-aggregation sequence is the defining downstream event of tau pathology in Alzheimer disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tau is not simply secreted; it accumulates intracellularly as tangles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lewy bodies are alpha-synuclein aggregates, not a tau structure.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the mislocalisation and aggregation of hyperphosphorylated tau into neurofibrillary tangles.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 19.

questions.title: Which genetic variant is described as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: Which genetic variant is described as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. ApoE2 is relatively protective against Alzheimer disease, the opposite of a risk factor.
explanations.B: Correct. Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) has three common alleles (E2, E3, E4). ApoE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset, sporadic Alzheimer disease, impairing Aβ clearance from the brain. It is a risk-modifying allele for the common sporadic form, distinct from the deterministic APP/presenilin mutations that cause rare familial disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ApoE3 is the population-average-risk allele, neither strongly protective nor a major risk factor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ApoA1 is a lipoprotein associated with HDL metabolism, not the recognised Alzheimer risk gene.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ApoE4 as the major genetic risk allele for sporadic Alzheimer disease.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 20.

questions.title: What is the effect of each ApoE4 allele on Alzheimer's disease risk?
questions.question: What is the effect of each ApoE4 allele on Alzheimer's disease risk?

explanations.A: Incorrect. ApoE4 increases, rather than decreases, risk.
explanations.B: Correct. ApoE4 confers risk in a gene-dose-dependent fashion: each copy of the E4 allele raises Alzheimer disease risk by roughly four-fold relative to the common ApoE3/E3 genotype, so a homozygote (E4/E4) carries substantially higher lifetime risk than a heterozygote. ApoE4 raises risk and lowers age of onset but neither guarantees disease nor is required for it — it is a risk modifier, not a deterministic cause.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ApoE4 has a well-established, substantial effect on risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ApoE4 raises risk; it does not prevent disease.

questions.learning_objective: Quantify ApoE4's effect on Alzheimer disease risk as approximately four-fold per allele.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 21.

questions.title: Which of the following is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly population?
questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly population?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vascular dementia is the second most common cause and frequently coexists with Alzheimer disease (mixed dementia), but it is not the leading cause.
explanations.B: Correct. Alzheimer disease accounts for the majority of dementia cases in older adults, more than vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies or frontotemporal dementia combined. This makes it the leading single cause of cognitive decline in this age group worldwide. Vascular dementia ranks second and frequently coexists with Alzheimer disease as mixed dementia, but does not overtake it in overall prevalence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dementia with Lewy bodies is a less common cause than Alzheimer disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Frontotemporal dementia is typically an earlier-onset, less common cause than Alzheimer disease in the elderly population overall.

questions.learning_objective: State that Alzheimer disease is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 22.

questions.title: What is the primary physiological role of tau protein in neurons?
questions.question: What is the primary physiological role of tau protein in neurons?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tau does not synthesise neurotransmitters.
explanations.B: Correct. In its normal state, tau is an axonal microtubule-associated protein that binds and stabilises microtubules, supporting axonal transport and cytoskeletal integrity. This normal binding function is lost once tau becomes hyperphosphorylated in Alzheimer disease, which is precisely why hyperphosphorylation disrupts axonal transport and neuronal function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tau is not a vesicle-release protein; that role belongs to proteins such as synaptotagmin and SNAREs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myelin formation is an oligodendrocyte/Schwann cell function, unrelated to tau.

questions.learning_objective: State tau's normal physiological role as a microtubule-binding/stabilising protein.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 24.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a gross morphological finding in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a gross morphological finding in Alzheimer's disease?

options.B: Cortical atrophy of frontal, temporal and parietal lobes

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a finding). Reduced brain weight is a typical gross Alzheimer finding.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a finding). Fronto-temporo-parietal cortical atrophy is the characteristic gross distribution.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a finding). Widened sulci accompany the cortical atrophy.
explanations.D: Correct. Alzheimer disease produces a characteristic gross pattern — reduced brain weight, widened cortical sulci and atrophy predominantly in the frontal, temporal and parietal association cortices. The cerebellum is relatively spared grossly, unlike the cerebrum; prominent cerebellar atrophy instead suggests a spinocerebellar or multisystem atrophy process, not typical Alzheimer disease.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cerebellar atrophy as NOT a typical gross finding of Alzheimer disease, distinguishing it from the expected fronto-temporo-parietal pattern.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 25.

questions.title: Which microscopic finding in Alzheimer's disease appears as focal spherical structures with a central amyloid core?
questions.question: Which microscopic finding in Alzheimer's disease appears as focal spherical structures with a central amyloid core?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neurofibrillary tangles are intracellular, tau-based structures, not extracellular amyloid-core spheres.
explanations.B: Correct. Neuritic (senile) plaques are extracellular, roughly spherical lesions in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus, consisting of a dense central core of aggregated beta-amyloid surrounded by dystrophic neurites and activated glia. They are one of the two defining microscopic lesions of Alzheimer disease, alongside neurofibrillary tangles. Plaque density and distribution are part of the standard neuropathological staging used to grade Alzheimer disease severity at autopsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lewy bodies are intracellular alpha-synuclein inclusions, a different structure entirely.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hirano bodies are intracellular actin-rich rod inclusions, not the amyloid-core plaque described here.

questions.learning_objective: Describe neuritic plaques as extracellular, amyloid-core lesions, one of Alzheimer disease's two hallmark microscopic findings.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 26.

questions.title: Neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease contain which abnormal protein?
questions.question: Neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease contain which abnormal protein?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Beta-amyloid forms the extracellular plaque core, not the intracellular tangle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alpha-synuclein forms Lewy bodies, a different inclusion from the neurofibrillary tangle.
explanations.C: Correct. Neurofibrillary tangles are intracellular, paired-helical-filament aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau protein that accumulate in the neuronal cell body and proximal dendrites, disrupting the cytoskeleton and axonal transport. Mixing up tangle composition (tau) with plaque composition (amyloid) is the single most common Alzheimer-histology error, so keeping the two separate is essential.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prion protein misfolding defines prion disease, unrelated to the neurofibrillary tangle.

questions.learning_objective: State that neurofibrillary tangles are composed of abnormal (hyperphosphorylated) tau, not amyloid, synuclein or prion protein.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 27.

questions.title: Which staining method is used to detect neurofibrillary tangles?
questions.question: Which staining method is used to detect neurofibrillary tangles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gram stain identifies bacteria, not tangles.
explanations.B: Correct. Neurofibrillary tangles are classically highlighted using silver impregnation stains (e.g. Bielschowsky or Bodian silver stain), which bind the paired helical filaments of aggregated tau and render tangles clearly visible by light microscopy; modern practice supplements this with tau-specific immunohistochemistry.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acid-fast stain identifies mycobacteria, not tangles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PAS stain identifies glycogen, fungi and basement membrane material, not tangles.

questions.learning_objective: Identify silver staining as the classic method for demonstrating neurofibrillary tangles.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 28.

questions.title: What is cerebral amyloid angiopathy?
questions.question: What is cerebral amyloid angiopathy?

options.B: Deposition of Aβ in the walls of cerebral blood vessels

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a deposition process, not primarily an inflammatory vasculitis.
explanations.B: Correct. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is beta-amyloid deposition within the media and adventitia of small-to-medium cerebral cortical and leptomeningeal arteries, weakening the vessel wall. It commonly coexists with Alzheimer disease, sharing its amyloid pathogenesis, and is an important cause of lobar intracerebral haemorrhage in older adults.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CAA is an arterial-wall amyloid deposition process, not venous thrombosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CAA weakens vessel walls diffusely via amyloid deposition rather than forming discrete aneurysms.

questions.learning_objective: Define cerebral amyloid angiopathy as vascular-wall beta-amyloid deposition, distinct from parenchymal plaque deposition.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a microscopic finding in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a microscopic finding in Alzheimer's disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a finding). Neuronal loss is core to Alzheimer disease microscopy.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a finding). Reactive gliosis accompanies the neuronal loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a finding). Neuritic plaques are a defining Alzheimer lesion.
explanations.D: Correct. The core microscopic findings of Alzheimer disease are neuronal loss, reactive gliosis and extracellular neuritic plaques, together with neurofibrillary tangles. White matter demyelination is not a defining Alzheimer feature — it is instead the hallmark of the separate demyelinating disease category, such as multiple sclerosis, a grey-matter-versus-white-matter distinction worth keeping clear.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude white matter demyelination from Alzheimer disease's defining microscopic findings.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 29.

questions.title: What cellular reaction accompanies neuronal loss in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: What cellular reaction accompanies neuronal loss in Alzheimer's disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Microglia are activated, not suppressed, in response to neuronal injury.
explanations.B: Correct. When neurons die in Alzheimer disease, astrocytes proliferate and hypertrophy in the affected region — reactive astrogliosis — as the standard CNS reparative/reactive response to neuronal injury, alongside microglial activation. Gliosis is a generic CNS injury response, not specific to Alzheimer disease, but it consistently accompanies neuronal loss wherever it occurs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Oligodendrocyte proliferation is not the characteristic reactive response to neuronal loss; astrogliosis is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Endothelial activation is not the defining cellular reaction to neuronal loss in Alzheimer disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that gliosis (reactive astrocyte proliferation) accompanies neuronal loss in Alzheimer disease.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 30.

questions.title: Which lobes characteristically show cortical atrophy in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: Which lobes characteristically show cortical atrophy in Alzheimer's disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The occipital lobe is not part of the classic early atrophy pattern; prominent occipital involvement instead suggests dementia with Lewy bodies or posterior cortical atrophy.
explanations.B: Correct. The gross cortical atrophy of Alzheimer disease follows a characteristic distribution: frontal, temporal (especially medial temporal/hippocampal) and parietal association cortices are disproportionately affected. The primary sensorimotor and occipital cortices are relatively spared until late disease. This regional pattern is why early, prominent occipital involvement instead points toward a different diagnosis such as dementia with Lewy bodies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This combination omits the frontal and temporal lobes and wrongly includes the occipital lobe.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This combination omits the temporal and parietal lobes and wrongly includes the occipital lobe.

questions.learning_objective: Name the frontal, temporal and parietal lobes as the sites of characteristic Alzheimer cortical atrophy.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 31.

questions.title: Which of the following is described as a coexisting neuropathology commonly seen with Alzheimer's disease?
questions.question: Which of the following is described as a coexisting neuropathology commonly seen with Alzheimer's disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. MS plaques are not a typical Alzheimer disease comorbidity.
explanations.B: Correct. Because Alzheimer disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy share the same beta-amyloid pathogenesis, the two conditions very frequently coexist. A substantial majority of Alzheimer disease brains show at least some degree of amyloid deposition in cortical/leptomeningeal vessel walls in addition to the parenchymal plaques and tangles. This coexistence matters clinically because it raises the risk of lobar intracerebral haemorrhage in these patients.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lewy bodies characterise a distinct disease (Parkinson/Lewy body disease), though mixed pathology can occur; it is not the classic coexisting finding being tested here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pick bodies characterise frontotemporal dementia (Pick disease), a separate tauopathy, not a typical Alzheimer coexisting finding.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise cerebral amyloid angiopathy as a common coexisting finding in Alzheimer disease, sharing its amyloid pathogenesis.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 32.

questions.title: Which of the following is a reversible cause of dementia that must be excluded in patient management?
questions.question: Which of the following is a reversible cause of dementia that must be excluded in patient management?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Huntington disease is an irreversible, degenerative genetic disorder.
explanations.B: Correct. Vitamin B12 (and less commonly thiamine or folate) deficiency can produce a dementia syndrome that improves or resolves with replacement therapy. Because it is treatable, vitamin deficiency is one of the standard causes screened for in any dementia work-up, alongside other reversible causes such as hypothyroidism and normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Missing this diagnosis denies the patient an effective, low-risk treatment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rapidly progressive, irreversible prion disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Frontotemporal dementia is an irreversible, degenerative tauopathy/TDP-43 proteinopathy.

questions.learning_objective: Identify vitamin deficiency as a reversible, screenable cause of dementia.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Reversible causes of dementia
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 33.

questions.title: Which endocrine disorder is a recognised reversible cause of dementia?
questions.question: Which endocrine disorder is a recognised reversible cause of dementia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism more typically causes anxiety/agitation than a dementia-like slowing picture.
explanations.B: Correct. Hypothyroidism can cause a cognitive-slowing/dementia-like syndrome that improves with thyroid hormone replacement, making thyroid function testing (TSH) a standard, low-cost component of the reversible-dementia screening work-up. It is the classic, high-yield reversible endocrine dementia cause.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cushing syndrome is not the classic reversible-dementia endocrine answer, though it can affect mood and cognition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Addison disease is not the classic reversible-dementia endocrine answer.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hypothyroidism as the endocrine disorder that is a reversible cause of dementia.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Reversible causes of dementia
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 34.

questions.title: What is the fundamental pathological process in demyelinating diseases?
questions.question: What is the fundamental pathological process in demyelinating diseases?

options.B: Damage to the myelin sheath of neurons

explanations.A: Incorrect. Demyelinating disease targets myelin, not primarily the neuronal cell body.
explanations.B: Correct. Demyelinating diseases are defined by injury targeted at the myelin sheath — the lipid-rich insulating wrap around axons produced by oligodendrocytes (CNS) or Schwann cells (PNS). This targets myelin rather than the neuronal cell body or axon itself, distinguishing demyelinating disease from primary neurodegenerative or axonal diseases. Axons and cell bodies can be secondarily affected only after repeated or prolonged demyelination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Synaptic loss is not the defining process; myelin damage is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While oligodendrocyte injury can occur (e.g. in PML), the fundamental process defining the disease category is myelin sheath damage itself, not oligodendrocyte apoptosis alone.

questions.learning_objective: State that myelin sheath damage, not neuronal cell body destruction, is the fundamental process in demyelinating disease.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 35.

questions.title: What is the primary functional consequence of myelin damage in demyelinating diseases?
questions.question: What is the primary functional consequence of myelin damage in demyelinating diseases?

options.B: Impaired conduction of signals in affected nerves

explanations.A: Incorrect. Myelin loss impairs, rather than enhances, signalling.
explanations.B: Correct. Myelin normally allows fast, saltatory conduction of action potentials by insulating the axon between nodes of Ranvier. When myelin is damaged, conduction slows, becomes unreliable, or fails (conduction block), producing the sensory, motor and visual symptoms characteristic of demyelinating disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Myelin loss impairs, rather than increases, effective synaptic function.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Demyelination does not accelerate axonal regeneration; it impairs conduction and can secondarily injure axons.

questions.learning_objective: Link myelin damage to impaired/slowed axonal conduction as the primary functional consequence.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 36.

questions.title: Which of the following is the defining characteristic of myelinoclastic demyelinating diseases?
questions.question: Which of the following is the defining characteristic of myelinoclastic demyelinating diseases?

options.B: Normal and healthy myelin is destroyed by toxic, chemical, or autoimmune substances
options.C: Myelin fails to form during development

explanations.A: Incorrect. Myelin abnormal from birth describes leukodystrophy, the opposite category.
explanations.B: Correct. Myelinoclastic (acquired) demyelinating diseases — multiple sclerosis being the prototype — destroy myelin that formed normally in the first place. The insult is acquired: toxic, metabolic or, most often, autoimmune, occurring after normal myelination was already complete. This is the opposite of leukodystrophy, in which myelin was never normal to begin with.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Failure of myelin formation during development describes leukodystrophy, not myelinoclastic disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Abnormal turnover kinetics is not the defining myelinoclastic mechanism; acquired destruction of previously normal myelin is.

questions.learning_objective: Define myelinoclastic disease as acquired destruction of previously normal myelin.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 37.

questions.title: What is the key difference between myelinoclastic and leukodystrophic diseases?
questions.question: What is the key difference between myelinoclastic and leukodystrophic diseases?

options.A: Myelinoclastic diseases affect only the PNS
options.B: In myelinoclastic diseases, myelin was normal before the disease; in leukodystrophic diseases, myelin was never normal

explanations.A: Incorrect. Myelinoclastic disease is not restricted to the PNS — multiple sclerosis, the prototype, is a CNS disease.
explanations.B: Correct. Leukodystrophies are inherited, typically enzymatic/metabolic disorders in which myelin is abnormally formed or maintained from the outset, whereas myelinoclastic diseases such as multiple sclerosis destroy myelin that had developed and functioned normally before the disease process began. This distinction underlies different imaging patterns, ages of onset and management approaches.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leukodystrophies are inherited/congenital, the reverse of 'always acquired'.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myelinoclastic disease is not restricted to childhood — multiple sclerosis typically presents in young adulthood.

questions.learning_objective: State the myelinoclastic-versus-leukodystrophic distinction: myelin normal-then-destroyed versus never-normal.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 38.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a clinical feature of demyelinating diseases?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a clinical feature of demyelinating diseases?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a feature). Ocular disturbances (e.g. optic neuritis, ophthalmoplegia) are classic demyelinating features.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a feature). Impaired coordination reflects cerebellar/proprioceptive pathway involvement.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a feature). Weakness reflects corticospinal tract involvement.
explanations.D: Correct. The classic clinical repertoire of CNS demyelinating disease includes ocular disturbances, impaired coordination and limb weakness from white matter lesions. Seizures are uncommon and not a standard teaching feature, since demyelinating lesions are predominantly white matter rather than the cortical grey matter that generates seizure activity; seizures can rarely occur if a lesion abuts the cortex, but are not a defining feature.

questions.learning_objective: Exclude seizures from the standard clinical feature list of demyelinating disease.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 39.

questions.title: In which brain region are myelinated axons the dominant component?
questions.question: In which brain region are myelinated axons the dominant component?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Grey matter is dominated by neuronal cell bodies, not myelinated axon tracts.
explanations.B: Correct. Cerebral white matter is composed predominantly of myelinated axons travelling between cortical regions and subcortical structures; its pale colour on gross examination comes directly from the lipid-rich myelin sheaths. This is why demyelinating disease characteristically produces white matter lesions, visible as plaques on imaging and at autopsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The basal ganglia are grey matter nuclei, not the white matter tract region being asked about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The hippocampus is a grey matter (cortical) structure, not the white matter compartment.

questions.learning_objective: Identify white matter as the brain compartment dominated by myelinated axons, explaining why it is the target of demyelinating disease.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 40.

questions.title: Which of the following is a demyelinating disease of the CNS?
questions.question: Which of the following is a demyelinating disease of the CNS?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Guillain-Barre syndrome is a PNS demyelinating disease, not a CNS one.
explanations.B: Correct. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is a monophasic, typically post-infectious or post-vaccination autoimmune demyelinating disease of the CNS. It causes widespread white matter inflammation and demyelination visible on brain and spinal cord MRI. This CNS localisation and typically monophasic course distinguish it from the PNS demyelinating diseases listed among the other options, and from the relapsing course of multiple sclerosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is an inherited PNS neuropathy (often a leukodystrophy-like/dysmyelinating peripheral process), not a CNS demyelinating disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is a PNS demyelinating disease, not a CNS one.

questions.learning_objective: Classify ADEM as a CNS (not PNS) demyelinating disease.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 41.

questions.title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is caused by what type of agent?
questions.question: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is caused by what type of agent?

explanations.A: Incorrect. PML is viral, not bacterial, in origin.
explanations.B: Correct. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by reactivation of JC virus (a polyomavirus) in immunocompromised patients, which lytically infects and destroys oligodendrocytes, producing multifocal demyelinating lesions of the CNS white matter — a viral, not autoimmune or toxic, demyelinating mechanism, occurring specifically in immunosuppressed hosts (e.g. advanced HIV, natalizumab therapy).
explanations.C: Incorrect. PML is not autoimmune-mediated, unlike multiple sclerosis or ADEM.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PML is not caused by toxic chemical exposure; it is a direct viral infection.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute PML to viral (JC virus) infection of oligodendrocytes, not autoimmune or toxic injury.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Demyelinating disease — general pathology
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 42.

questions.title: What is the approximate prevalence of multiple sclerosis in the United States and Europe?
questions.question: What is the approximate prevalence of multiple sclerosis in the United States and Europe?

explanations.A: Incorrect. This overstates MS prevalence roughly ten-fold.
explanations.B: Correct. Multiple sclerosis affects roughly 1 in 1000 people in high-prevalence regions such as the United States and Europe. This reflects a latitude-linked prevalence gradient, with higher rates farther from the equator. The gradient is attributed to a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental factors such as vitamin D exposure and past Epstein-Barr virus infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This understates MS prevalence roughly ten-fold for these high-prevalence regions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This understates MS prevalence roughly one-hundred-fold for these high-prevalence regions.

questions.learning_objective: State the approximate MS prevalence figure (about 1 per 1000) for the US and Europe.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 43.

questions.title: Which statement about the epidemiology of MS is CORRECT?
questions.question: Which statement about the epidemiology of MS is CORRECT?

options.A: Men are affected twice as often as women
options.B: Women are affected twice as often as men

explanations.A: Incorrect. This reverses the true sex ratio.
explanations.B: Correct. Multiple sclerosis shows a clear female predominance, with women affected roughly twice as frequently as men. This sex disparity is attributed to hormonal and immune-system differences between men and women. MS is one of the classic female-predominant autoimmune diseases, alongside conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A real, well-documented sex difference exists.
explanations.D: Incorrect. MS affects both sexes, though women more often.

questions.learning_objective: State the approximately 2:1 female-to-male sex ratio in multiple sclerosis.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 44.

questions.title: At what ages is onset of MS relatively rare?
questions.question: At what ages is onset of MS relatively rare?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 20-30 years falls within the typical, not rare, onset window.
explanations.B: Correct. Multiple sclerosis characteristically begins between the late teens and about age 40-50, with onset in childhood or after age 50 being comparatively uncommon. Late-onset MS, when it occurs, tends to have a more progressive course from the outset compared with the relapsing-remitting pattern typical of young-adult-onset disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 30-40 years falls within the typical, not rare, onset window.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 40-50 years is at the upper edge of, but still within, the typical onset window rather than the classically 'rare' extremes.

questions.learning_objective: State that MS onset is relatively rare in childhood and after age 50, being typically a young-adult-onset disease.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 45.

questions.title: What is the characteristic clinical course of MS in most patients?
questions.question: What is the characteristic clinical course of MS in most patients?

options.B: Relapsing and remitting episodes of neurologic impairment
options.D: Acute fulminant course leading to early death

explanations.A: Incorrect. Steady progression without remission from onset describes primary progressive MS, a minority pattern.
explanations.B: Correct. The majority of multiple sclerosis patients present with relapsing-remitting MS. This course consists of discrete attacks of new or worsening neurological symptoms, followed by partial or complete recovery, rather than steady unremitting progression from onset. Many relapsing-remitting patients later transition into a secondary progressive phase, in which disability accumulates even between relapses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A single monophasic episode describes clinically isolated syndrome or ADEM, not typical MS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. MS is not typically a fulminant, rapidly fatal disease.

questions.learning_objective: State relapsing-remitting disease as the characteristic clinical course for most MS patients.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Multiple sclerosis — clinical course
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 46.

questions.title: What happens to the frequency of relapses during the course of MS?
questions.question: What happens to the frequency of relapses during the course of MS?

options.D: It becomes more severe but less frequent

explanations.A: Incorrect. Relapse frequency does not steadily increase over the disease course.
explanations.B: Correct. Population-level natural-history data show that relapse frequency tends to decline as MS duration increases, even as many patients transition toward a more steadily progressive phase (secondary progressive MS) with accumulating disability despite fewer distinct relapses. A falling relapse rate does not mean improving disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Relapse frequency is not constant; it tends to decline over time.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This overstates a change in severity that is not the characterised pattern; the tested fact is frequency declining, not severity increasing.

questions.learning_objective: State that relapse frequency in MS tends to decrease over the course of the disease.
questions.module_subject: ASU-CNS-2 > Pathology > Multiple sclerosis — clinical course
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 47.

questions.title: MS is described as an autoimmune disease caused by loss of tolerance to what?
questions.question: MS is described as an autoimmune disease caused by loss of tolerance to what?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The primary autoimmune target is myelin, not the neuronal cell body directly.
explanations.B: Correct. Multiple sclerosis pathogenesis begins with a breakdown of self-tolerance to myelin. Autoreactive T cells, and subsequently B cells and antibodies, target myelin antigens such as myelin basic protein and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein. This autoimmune attack drives the inflammatory demyelination that defines the disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Astrocytes are not the primary autoimmune target in MS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Microglia are not the primary autoimmune target in MS; they participate in the inflammatory response but are not the self-antigen being attacked.

questions.learning_objective: State that MS is autoimmune, driven by loss of tolerance to myelin (self-protein) antigens.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 48.

questions.title: What is the disease risk for MS when it is present in a first-degree relative?
questions.question: What is the disease risk for MS when it is present in a first-degree relative?

explanations.A: Incorrect. This understates the true familial risk increase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This understates the true familial risk increase.
explanations.C: Correct. Multiple sclerosis shows significant familial clustering. The risk to a first-degree relative of an affected individual is roughly 15 times the general-population risk. This reflects a strong genetic contribution — chiefly HLA-linked, see the companion pathology fact — layered on top of environmental triggers.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This overstates the true familial risk increase, and would approach the magnitude seen only in much more strongly Mendelian conditions.

questions.learning_objective: Quantify first-degree-relative MS risk at approximately 15-fold over baseline.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 49.

questions.title: What is the concordance rate for MS in monozygotic twins?
questions.question: What is the concordance rate for MS in monozygotic twins?

explanations.A: Incorrect. This understates the true monozygotic concordance rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This understates the true monozygotic concordance rate.
explanations.C: Correct. Monozygotic (identical) twin studies show an MS concordance rate of roughly 25%, far higher than the population risk and higher than dizygotic twin or sibling concordance. This confirms a substantial genetic contribution to disease risk. Because the rate is well short of 100%, environmental factors must also be required to actually trigger disease, even in a genetically identical co-twin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This overstates the true monozygotic concordance rate — a figure this high would imply a near-deterministic single-gene cause, which is not the case for MS.

questions.learning_objective: State the approximate 25% monozygotic twin concordance rate for MS, and what it implies about gene-environment interaction.

questions.title: Which HLA association is implicated in the pathogenesis of MS?
questions.question: Which HLA association is implicated in the pathogenesis of MS?

explanations.A: Incorrect. HLA-B27 is associated with the spondyloarthropathies, not MS.
explanations.B: Correct. The strongest and most consistently replicated genetic association in multiple sclerosis is with HLA-DR, specifically HLA-DRB1*15:01 in most populations studied. HLA-DR is a class II MHC molecule that presents myelin peptide antigens to CD4+ T cells. This mechanistically links the genetic risk factor to the disease's autoimmune, CD4+-T-cell-mediated pathogenesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. HLA-A3 is a class I allele associated with hereditary haemochromatosis, not the classic MS association.
explanations.D: Incorrect. HLA-DQ shows some MS association in certain populations but HLA-DR is the primary, classically taught association.

questions.learning_objective: State the HLA-DR association with multiple sclerosis susceptibility.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 50.

questions.title: Which T cell subset is described as having a central role in MS pathogenesis?
questions.question: Which T cell subset is described as having a central role in MS pathogenesis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. CD3 is a pan-T-cell marker, not specific to the pathogenic subset being tested.
explanations.B: Correct. Autoreactive CD4+ (helper) T cells, activated against myelin antigens and presented via HLA-DR, are considered central drivers of MS pathogenesis. They orchestrate the inflammatory cascade that recruits macrophages, activates microglia and ultimately triggers demyelination. This fits the class II, CD4-restricted, HLA-DR genetic association described in the companion pathogenesis fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CD20 marks B cells, not T cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CD45 is a pan-leukocyte marker, not specific to the pathogenic T cell subset.

questions.learning_objective: Identify CD4+ T cells as the immune cell subset with the central pathogenic role in MS.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 51.

questions.title: What is the gross appearance of MS plaques?
questions.question: What is the gross appearance of MS plaques?

options.B: Well-circumscribed, slightly depressed, glassy-appearing, gray-tan lesions

explanations.A: Incorrect. Soft, pink, well-vascularised describes a highly vascular lesion (e.g. a tumour), not a demyelinating plaque.
explanations.B: Correct. On gross pathological examination, MS plaques are sharply demarcated lesions, often slightly sunken relative to surrounding white matter. They have a translucent, glassy, grey-tan appearance. This colour and texture change reflects the loss of the normal white, lipid-rich myelin in that area.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Haemorrhagic/necrotic describes an infarct or haemorrhage, not the classic MS plaque appearance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cystic, fluid-filled cavities describe an old infarct or cyst, not the glassy, solid MS plaque.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the gross appearance of MS plaques as well-circumscribed, glassy, grey-tan lesions.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 52.

questions.title: Where do MS plaques commonly arise?
questions.question: Where do MS plaques commonly arise?

explanations.A: Incorrect. MS is a white matter disease affecting many sites, not confined to the cortex (grey matter).
explanations.B: Correct. MS plaques show a characteristic predilection for periventricular white matter. They also commonly involve the optic nerves, brainstem, cerebellum and spinal cord. This periventricular distribution is exploited diagnostically on MRI, seen as periventricular ovoid lesions ('Dawson fingers').
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cerebellum is a common but not exclusive site; periventricular white matter is the more classically emphasised location.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spinal cord is a common but not exclusive site; MS is a multifocal, disseminated disease.

questions.learning_objective: State the periventricular predilection of MS plaque location.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 53.

questions.title: What is found in active MS plaques at the microscopic level?
questions.question: What is found in active MS plaques at the microscopic level?

options.B: Evidence of ongoing myelin breakdown with abundant macrophages containing myelin debris

explanations.A: Incorrect. Red blood cells alone would describe a haemorrhage, not an active demyelinating plaque.
explanations.B: Correct. In an actively demyelinating MS lesion, macrophages and activated microglia infiltrate the plaque and phagocytose breakdown products of degraded myelin. Macrophages laden with myelin debris are therefore the histological hallmark of lesion activity. Their presence distinguishes an active plaque from a chronic, inactive (burnt-out, gliotic) plaque, which lacks this ongoing phagocytic activity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neuronal cell bodies alone do not describe the inflammatory, myelin-breakdown picture of an active plaque.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Normal myelin with no inflammation is the opposite of an active lesion — it would describe unaffected white matter.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the microscopic hallmark of an active MS plaque: macrophages containing myelin debris amid ongoing myelin breakdown.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 54.

questions.title: What is the characteristic arrangement of lymphocytes and macrophages in active MS lesions?
questions.question: What is the characteristic arrangement of lymphocytes and macrophages in active MS lesions?

options.C: Only at the center of the lesion

explanations.A: Incorrect. The arrangement is not random; it follows a specific, named pattern.
explanations.B: Correct. Active MS lesions show inflammatory cells characteristically arranged as sleeve-like aggregates surrounding small veins and venules, known as perivascular cuffing. This arrangement reflects the route by which these cells cross the blood-brain barrier to enter the CNS parenchyma. Once inside, they drive the demyelination that defines the lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inflammatory cells are not confined to the lesion centre; the perivascular pattern is the defining feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inflammatory cells are not confined exclusively to the periphery; they cuff vessels distributed through the lesion.

questions.learning_objective: Describe perivascular cuffing as the characteristic arrangement of inflammatory cells in active MS lesions.
questions.source_citation: Ain Shams Year 2 CNS "MCQs - Neurodegenerative_Diseases.pdf", item 55.

questions.title: What is the state of axons within MS plaques?
questions.question: What is the state of axons within MS plaques?

options.B: Relatively preserved but may be reduced in number

explanations.A: Incorrect. Complete destruction overstates axonal involvement, which is secondary to the primary myelin-directed process.
explanations.B: Correct. Although MS is primarily a demyelinating disease, axons within a plaque are relatively — not completely — preserved. Some axonal loss and transection does occur, particularly with chronic or repeated demyelination, and this contributes to permanent disability. The axon is not, however, the primary initial target of the disease process the way myelin is.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Axons do not proliferate in MS plaques; neurons and axons do not typically regenerate by proliferation in the adult CNS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Remyelination is often incomplete, which is why plaques persist and disability can accumulate — 'completely' remyelinated overstates the typical outcome.

questions.learning_objective: State that MS-plaque axons are relatively preserved (though possibly reduced in number), not completely destroyed or fully regenerated.
